extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, students of biology, and educated general readers interested in evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter explaining the principle of natural selection and sexual selection, the conditions that favour or hinder their action, and illustrative examples showing how selection operates on organisms, ages, sexes, and minor characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Natural Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations; variations neither useful nor injurious are left as fluctuating elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because more individuals are born than can possibly survive, any slight advantage gives better chance of surviving and procreating; thus natural selection preserves favourable differences and eliminates injurious ones. Examples and contrasts with man’s selection are given to illustrate how slight advantages accumulate over long periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions favourable to Natural Selection: isolation (limited immigration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas partly or wholly surrounded by barriers (e.g., islands) give natural selection 'free scope' because new and better-adapted forms cannot freely immigrate to fill vacant places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an area is open to immigration, vacant ecological places would be seized by intruders; in isolated areas, slight modifications that give any advantage tend to be preserved and accumulated. Example: islands or countries with barriers where modification of natives can fill unoccupied places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions favourable to Natural Selection: change in conditions increases variability
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in the conditions of life, especially when acting on the reproductive system, causes or increases variability and so favours natural selection by increasing the chance of profitable variations occurring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not an extreme amount of variability is necessary; because nature has far longer time than man, even small individual differences accumulated can produce great results. Change of conditions thus aids selection by producing more variation on which it can act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality of intercrossing and its bearing on selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Intercrosses between individuals of the same species are common; intercrossing is listed among circumstances favourable and unfavourable to natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter flags intercrossing as a key circumstance affecting selection (it appears in the chapter heading), implying that rates of interbreeding influence how variation is expressed and how selection can operate, though detailed treatment appears elsewhere in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of population size and number of individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of individuals in a species influences the action of natural selection—large or small stocks affect preservation and extinction dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large local stocks can be necessary for preservation (example: crops vs garden plants and birds eating seed); small populations may be unable to produce seed or survive. The heading mentions 'number of individuals' as a circumstance affecting selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow, cumulative action of Natural Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection acts slowly over long geological periods, accumulating slight advantageous changes to produce large results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We see little of these changes in progress because they are extremely slow; nature's longer timescale compared to man's explains greater perfection of natural products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection acts on characters of trifling importance and at all ages and on both sexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even apparently trivial characters (colour tints, down on fruit, small morphological differences) can be subject to selection; selection can act at any age and on either sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: leaf-eating insects being green, ptarmigan white in winter, subtle fruit-skin differences affecting beetle attack. Heritable changes that appear at particular life stages tend to reappear at that stage, allowing selection to act age-specifically (e.g., larval adaptations, seed traits, horns in adults).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual Selection (distinct mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual selection depends on a struggle between males for possession of females (or female choice); it differs from natural selection because it concerns success in mating rather than survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual selection is generally less rigorous than natural selection; it may favour weapons (horns, spurs), courage, ornament, singing, or other traits that improve mating success. Examples include male-male combat in stag-beetles, salmon, and alligators, and female choice in birds (birds of paradise, rock-thrush). Sexual selection can produce traits attached mainly to one sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection acts on internal and non-visible traits as well as visible ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike man, nature can act on every internal organ, constitutional difference, and the whole machinery of life, not merely external visible characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Man selects mainly for visible traits and often protects inferior individuals; nature can refine internal systems and exercise each selected character in fitting conditions, producing more 'true' adaptations over long periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of growth and correlated modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When one part of the organisation is modified through variation and accumulated by natural selection, laws of correlation of growth will cause other, often unexpected modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural selection must ensure that correlated modifications are not injurious; selection may indirectly produce adult features as correlated results of larval changes (and vice versa). Examples: larval adaptations affecting adult structure in insects that live briefly as adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition: severe among conspecifics and close allies
rubrics_metrics.description: The struggle for existence is almost invariably most severe between individuals of the same species and often between species of the same genus, because they use the same resources and face the same dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: varieties sown together (some varieties supplant others), crops mixing losing weaker varieties, one species of swallow supplanting another, rat species replacing another across climates. This severe competition explains local dominance and replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate often acts indirectly via effects on other species
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate generally acts mainly by favouring other species rather than directly causing success or failure of a species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: many garden plants can endure local climate but never naturalize because they cannot compete with natives or resist native animals; introduction of a single tree species altered plant and bird communities on a heath; subtle indirect webs of interactions link climate, plants, insects, and birds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population-density effects: epidemics and parasite-host dynamics as checks
rubrics_metrics.description: When a species becomes very numerous in a tract, epidemics or parasite increases often ensue and act as limiting checks independent of direct struggle for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: game animals showing epidemics, parasitic worms becoming disproportionally favoured where hosts are crowded; parasite-prey dynamics introduce secondary struggles (between parasite and prey) and complex checks at different life stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of sufficient local numbers and benefit of intercrossing
rubrics_metrics.description: A large local stock of individuals of the same species is sometimes necessary for its preservation; frequent intercrossing is beneficial while close interbreeding is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: difficulty obtaining seed from solitary garden plants; rare plants being abundant only where many individuals occur together; social plants surviving at range limits due to population clustering. The author notes but does not elaborate the roles of intercrossing and inbreeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection works for the good of the being, not to benefit other species
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection cannot modify a species in a manner that confers no advantage to itself merely for the good of another species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some historical natural-history statements suggest otherwise, the author could not find a case where a structure evolved solely for another species' benefit; selection favours traits that enhance the organism's own survival or reproductive success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence of Character and Extinction as outcomes of Natural Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection, through divergence of character and extinction, acts on descendants from a common parent and helps explain the grouping of all organic beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a corollary and part of the chapter's scope: selection can cause species to diverge as they adapt to different niches and can also lead to extinction of less-adapted forms; these processes contribute to taxonomic groupings (elaborated further elsewhere in the book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection can act on discrete inherited tendencies or innate behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual offspring may be born with innate tendencies to pursue certain prey or behaviours; such tendencies can be subject to selection just as morphological traits are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a wolf cub with a tendency to pursue particular prey could be favoured if that prey becomes more abundant. Analogies drawn to domesticated animals showing distinct behavioural tendencies (cats preferring rats vs mice).
